title: Surge-and-Stall-triage-blueprint-for-api-degradations
body:
Purpose:
This is a working triage blueprint for on-call responders when Redwood API surfaces sudden degradations we label as 'Surge' (large traffic/rate spike or bursty patterns causing saturation) and 'Stall' (increased timeouts, degraded streaming, or elevated error rates without clear traffic spike). Use this when alerts trigger for p95/p99 latency jumps, 429s >+500% baseline, streaming stalls, or error-rate anomalies.

Scope and intent:
- Covers first-response to frontend API symptoms and runtime-serving degradation patterns.
- Prioritizes quick mitigations to restore customer-facing behavior over full RCAs.
- Includes operator notes, concrete commands, dashboards to check, and escalation paths.
- NOT a detailed RCA — turn this into a postmortem checklist after stability is recovered.

Quick signals (single-pane check):
- Alerts: ALERT(api.latency.p99 > 2s sustained 5m), ALERT(api.429.rate > 10rps aggregated), ALERT(runtime.stream.stalled > 3 mins).
- Dashboards to open: "API: latency & errors" (p50/p95/p99), "Ingress: 429/Rate" (per-route), "Serving: queue depth & GPU utilization", and "Streaming: active_sessions, recv_bytes/sec, last_ack_timestamp".
- Top-of-triage check (3 bullets):
  1) Is the symptom global or region-specific? (region dropdown on console dashboards)
  2) Is there a correlation with deployments or config changes in the last 30m? (check "deployments" and CI/CD activity)
  3) Are upstream providers (model backends, cloud region APIs) reporting incidents?

First 10-minute checklist (for the on-call responder):
- Set status: create a short incident channel (#ops-incident-<id>) and post a one-line summary.
- Silence flapping alerts for 15m.
- Identify scope: run two queries:
- curl from a neutral worker to the API endpoint used by alerting (cheap synthetic). Example:
    curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://api.redwood.example/v1/health?show=latency
- Quick k8s/infra check: kubectl get pods -n runtime -o wide | egrep "CrashLoop|ImagePullBackOff|Evicted"
- Check current autoscaling behavior: look at autoscaler events and queue length (keda / custom autoscaler logs).

Diagnostic matrix by failure mode
1) Timeouts / slow p95-p99 latency jumps
   Likely causes: saturation (batching/queueing), kernel-level backpressure, long-model evals on some nodes, cross-region routing issues.
   Quick probes:
   - Query per-backend latency: query runtime.metrics.backend.latency{job="runtime"} by host.
   - Check GPU/CPU hot nodes: top pods by cpu/gpu: kubectl top pod -n runtime --containers | sort -nr -k2 | head
   - Look at queueing: runtime.request.queue.depth and per-worker accept rate.
   Immediate mitigations:
   - Enable emergency autoscale/burst policy (console -> Dedicated -> Force-burst capacity).
   - Reduce max-concurrency for heavy routes: set route-level concurrency cap to 1 or 2 to avoid head-of-line blocking.
   - Switch traffic to cheaper, lower-latency model variant or smaller sequence-length cap via routing policy.
   - If degradation is due to cold-start noise, enable warm cache or temporarily increase minimum replica count.

2) 429 surge (rate limits / quotas triggered)
   Likely causes: traffic burst from a customer, misbehaving client, telemetry loop, security scanning, or quota misconfiguration.
   Quick probes:
   - Identify top offenders: query logs for clients with highest 429 counts (by API key/client_id).
   - Check global quota config and recent changes (console -> quotas).
   - Inspect WAF or API gateway changes that could be returning 429 prematurely.
   Immediate mitigations:
   - Apply per-key emergency overrides: temporarily raise quota for affected production keys if they are legitimate customers.
   - Implement short-term global throttling: enable global backpressure to shed low-priority routes.
   - If caused by a loop/bot, use IP blocking rules at edge for the offending IP ranges.
   - Add temporary 429->retry-after header guidance and increase clients' retry window in client libraries.

3) Degraded streaming (stalls, partial frames, missing chunks)
   Likely causes: connection-level congestion, proxy buffering, heartbeat timeouts, or model runtime stalls.
   Quick probes:
   - Check streaming error patterns: gateway error codes, last_ack_timestamp per-session, and TCP retransmit rates on hosts.
   - Reproduce with a short synthetic streaming call from an internal worker, capturing timing and frames.
   - Check reverse-proxy/edge buffer settings for changes (nginx/ingress).
   Immediate mitigations:
   - Bump keepalive/idle timeouts on proxy to avoid premature TCP/TLS closes.
   - Flip traffic to a non-buffering path (edge -> raw TCP streaming) if available.
   - If stalls originate in runtime, temporarily disable long-lived streaming (fallback to chunked polling) and surface graceful degraded behavior to clients.

4) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes)
   Likely causes: resource exhaustion, dependency failures (KV store, external APIs), new bug from a deploy.
   Quick probes:
   - Correlate errors to deploys: last deploy window and commit IDs.
   - Inspect error logs for stack traces and anomaly patterns (same stacktrace across hosts implies code issue).
   - Check dependency health: redis/kv, model server, control-plane APIs.
   Immediate mitigations:
   - Rollback suspect deployment if errors line up with a release.
   - Apply circuit breakers: for a failing downstream dependency, short-circuit to fallback responses or reduced feature flags.
   - Enable additional retries with exponential backoff only for idempotent routes.

Short-term operator commands (grab-and-run snippets)
- Check top-latency hosts (promql):
  topk(5, increase(api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="1"}[5m]))
- Identify top 429 clients (logs):
  gcloud logging read "resource.type=container AND textPayload:\"429\"" --limit 50 --project redwood-prod
- Force route concurrency cap via CLI: redwoodctl routes update --id <route> --max-concurrency 2
- Temporarily scale workers: kubectl scale deploy/runtime-worker --replicas=8 -n runtime

Escalation path and contact list
- Primary on-call (SRE): whoever accepted the pager.
- If runtime-level resource issue suspected -> ping runtime infra leads: @Marcus Li, @Priya Desai.
- Model/backend infra -> ping Applied ML: @Evan Martinez.
- For customer-impacting outages (>= 10% customers or SLA breach): page on-call PM and GEM (pager) and follow incident comms template.

Incident comms template (short):
- Subject: [INCID-<id>] API degradation: <short-symptom>
- TL;DR: start_time, scope (regions/customers), immediate mitigation, user impact.
- What we're doing now: 1-2 bullets.
- Next update: in 15 minutes / when rollback completes.

Post-stabilization checklist
- Capture timestamps: when first alert, mitigation, and full recovery occurred.
- Freeze relevant logs and export top 1,000 requests during incident window for replay.
- Run RCA template: list of contributing factors, why defenses failed (autoscale thresholds, missing circuit breakers, inadequate break-glass).
- Follow-up actions (owner, priority): example: "increase route-specific concurrency visibility" (owner: Priya, P2, due 2 weeks).

Known gaps & unresolved questions (working list)
- Can the autoscaler detect queue-head-of-line blocking across heterogeneous model sizes? (investigate with runtime team).
- We lack a per-route synthetic streaming probe that emulates partial-frame stalls (nice-to-have).
- Better visibility at edge for per-client 429 attribution (add request-id and client-id propagation).

Scratchpad notes (operator hints):
- If you see p99 latency but p95 is fine, look for tail latencies in a handful of hosts: not global.
- A sudden rise in queued requests with flat throughput usually means some hosts are saturated/poisoned.
- For streaming issues, the first check is whether the client is receiving partial data (indicates buffering) vs. not receiving anything (connection drops).

Open TODOs for this document:
- Add step-by-step rollback play for Blue/Green with CLI snippets.
- Add example Slack comms and canned customer status page language.
- Add automated runbook linkouts from PagerDuty alerts to this doc.

If you update this document: append with initials and date and a 1-line summary of the change.

——
Authors / quick credits: Lin Wei (owner), input from Priya Desai (autoscaling heuristics), Evan Martinez (runtime streaming diagnostics), Marcus Li (edge & rate-limiting).

Unresolved: should we introduce an "emergency degraded-mode" that responds to upstream model stalls with reduced-quality but stable responses? (Discuss SRE + product)
